claim: Filamentous cyanobacteria are one of the oldest and today still most abundant lifeforms on earth.
source: Filamentous cyanobacteria are one of the oldest and today still most abundant lifeforms on earth, with manifold implications in ecology and economics.
evidence: This is a statement about the evolutionary history and current abundance of filamentous cyanobacteria, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Filamentous cyanobacteria have manifold implications in ecology and economics.
source: Filamentous cyanobacteria are one of the oldest and today still most abundant lifeforms on earth, with manifold implications in ecology and economics.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about the ecological and economic impacts of cyanobacteria.

claim: Filamentous cyanobacteria flexible filaments are often several hundred cells long.
source: Their flexible filaments, often several hundred cells long, exhibit gliding motility in contact with solid surfaces.
evidence: This is a descriptive observation about the physical characteristics of the organisms studied, supported by established knowledge.

claim: Filamentous cyanobacteria exhibit gliding motility in contact with solid surfaces.
source: Their flexible filaments, often several hundred cells long, exhibit gliding motility in contact with solid surfaces.
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of filamentous cyanobacteria, supported by scientific knowledge.

claim: The force generating mechanism underlying gliding motility in filamentous cyanobacteria is not yet understood.
source: The underlying force generating mechanism is not yet understood.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of scientific knowledge about the mechanism.

claim: Propulsion forces and friction coefficients are strongly coupled in the gliding motility of filamentous cyanobacteria.
source: Here, we demonstrate that propulsion forces and friction coefficients are strongly coupled in the gliding motility of filamentous cyanobacteria.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Bending moduli of filamentous cyanobacteria can be directly measured using micropipette force sensors.
source: We directly measure their bending moduli using micropipette force sensors, and quantify propulsion and friction forces by analyzing their self-buckling behavior, complemented with analytical theory and simulations.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Propulsion and friction forces can be quantified by analyzing self-buckling behavior of filamentous cyanobacteria.
source: We directly measure their bending moduli using micropipette force sensors, and quantify propulsion and friction forces by analyzing their self-buckling behavior, complemented with analytical theory and simulations.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach used in the study to derive force measurements.

claim: Slime extrusion is unlikely to generate the gliding forces in filamentous cyanobacteria.
source: The results indicate that slime extrusion unlikely generates the gliding forces, but support adhesion-based hypotheses, similar to the better-studied single-celled myxobacteria.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental results showing strong coupling between propulsion and friction forces.

claim: The results support adhesion-based hypotheses for gliding motility, similar to myxobacteria.
source: The results indicate that slime extrusion unlikely generates the gliding forces, but support adhesion-based hypotheses, similar to the better-studied single-celled myxobacteria.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data and comparison with known mechanisms in myxobacteria.

claim: The critical self-buckling lengths align well with the peaks of natural length distributions.
source: The critical self-buckling lengths align well with the peaks of natural length distributions, indicating the importance of self-buckling for the organization of their collective in natural and artificial settings.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of measured critical lengths with observed length distributions.

claim: Self-buckling is important for the organization of filamentous cyanobacteria collectives in natural and artificial settings.
source: The critical self-buckling lengths align well with the peaks of natural length distributions, indicating the importance of self-buckling for the organization of their collective in natural and artificial settings.
evidence: This is inferred from the alignment between critical buckling lengths and natural length distributions.

claim: Filamentous cyanobacteria contributed majorly to the global fixation of atmospheric carbon dioxide.
source: Filamentous cyanobacteria are an omnipresent group of phototrophic prokaryotes, contributing majorly to the global fixation of atmospheric carbon dioxide.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the ecological role of cyanobacteria.

claim: Filamentous cyanobacteria played an important role in generating atmospheric oxygen in Earth's paleoclimate.
source: They played an important role already in the paleoclimate of our planet, having generated the atmospheric oxygen (Whitton, 2012; Sciuto and Moro, 2015) on which animal life is based.
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific literature on the paleoclimate role of cyanobacteria.

claim: Animal life is based on atmospheric oxygen generated by cyanobacteria.
source: They played an important role already in the paleoclimate of our planet, having generated the atmospheric oxygen (Whitton, 2012; Sciuto and Moro, 2015) on which animal life is based.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the evolution of life on Earth, supported by citations.

claim: Giant marine and limnic cyanobacterial blooms pose ecological and economical threats.
source: Today, giant marine and limnic blooms pose ecological and economical threats (Whitton, 2012; Sciuto and Moro, 2015; Bauer et al., 2020; Fastner et al., 2018), but also enable bioreactor applications, for instance as a renewable energy source (Whitton, 2012; Ruffing and Kallas, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to scientific literature on cyanobacterial blooms.

claim: Cyanobacterial blooms enable bioreactor applications as a renewable energy source.
source: Today, giant marine and limnic blooms pose ecological and economical threats (Whitton, 2012; Sciuto and Moro, 2015; Bauer et al., 2020; Fastner et al., 2018), but also enable bioreactor applications, for instance as a renewable energy source (Whitton, 2012; Ruffing and Kallas, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific literature on bioreactor applications.

claim: Filamentous cyanobacteria contain up to several hundred linearly stacked cells.
source: The long and flexible filaments contain up to several hundred, linearly stacked cells.
evidence: This is a descriptive observation about the structure of filamentous cyanobacteria.

claim: Many species of filamentous cyanobacteria exhibit gliding motility when in contact with solid surfaces or other filaments.
source: Many species exhibit gliding motility when in contact with solid surfaces or other filaments, but no swimming motion (Burkholder, 1934).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to scientific literature on cyanobacterial motility.

claim: Filamentous cyanobacteria do not exhibit swimming motion.
source: Many species exhibit gliding motility when in contact with solid surfaces or other filaments, but no swimming motion (Burkholder, 1934).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to scientific literature on cyanobacterial motility.

claim: Motility enables filaments to aggregate into colonies.
source: Motility enables filaments to aggregate into colonies, adapting their architecture to environmental conditions (Whitton, 2012; Khayatan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific literature on cyanobacterial colony formation.

claim: Filamentous cyanobacteria adapt their colony architecture to environmental conditions.
source: Motility enables filaments to aggregate into colonies, adapting their architecture to environmental conditions (Whitton, 2012; Khayatan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific literature on cyanobacterial colony behavior.

claim: Slime extrusion has been proposed as a force generating mechanism for cyanobacterial gliding.
source: Slime extrusion (Hoiczyk and Baumeister, 1998), metachronal waves on surface fibrils (Halfen and Castenholz, 1971; Halfen, 1973; Read et al., 2007), and acoustic streaming (Koiller et al., 2010) have been proposed.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to scientific literature proposing this mechanism.

claim: Metachronal waves on surface fibrils have been proposed as a force generating mechanism for cyanobacterial gliding.
source: Slime extrusion (Hoiczyk and Baumeister, 1998), metachronal waves on surface fibrils (Halfen and Castenholz, 1971; Halfen, 1973; Read et al., 2007), and acoustic streaming (Koiller et al., 2010) have been proposed.
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific literature proposing this mechanism.

claim: Acoustic streaming has been proposed as a force generating mechanism for cyanobacterial gliding.
source: Slime extrusion (Hoiczyk and Baumeister, 1998), metachronal waves on surface fibrils (Halfen and Castenholz, 1971; Halfen, 1973; Read et al., 2007), and acoustic streaming (Koiller et al., 2010) have been proposed.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to scientific literature proposing this mechanism.

claim: A few species of filamentous cyanobacteria appear to employ a type-IV-pilus-related mechanism.
source: A few species appear to employ a type-IV-pilus-related mechanism (Khayatan et al., 2015; Wilde and Mullineaux, 2015), similar to the better-studied myxobacteria (Godwin et al., 1989; Mignot et al., 2007; Nan et al., 2014; Copenhagen et al., 2021; Godwin et al., 1989), which are short, rod-shaped single cells that exhibit two types of motility: S (social) motility based on pilus extension and retraction, and A (adventurous) motility based on focal adhesion (Chen and Nan, 2022), for which also slime extrusion at the trailing cell pole was earlier postulated as mechanism (Wolgemuth, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific literature on type-IV pilus mechanisms.

claim: Myxobacteria are short, rod-shaped single cells that exhibit two types of motility: S (social) motility and A (adventurous) motility.
source: A few species appear to employ a type-IV-pilus-related mechanism (Khayatan et al., 2015; Wilde and Mullineaux, 2015), similar to the better-studied myxobacteria (Godwin et al., 1989; Mignot et al., 2007; Nan et al., 2014; Copenhagen et al., 2021; Godwin et al., 1989), which are short, rod-shaped single cells that exhibit two types of motility: S (social) motility based on pilus extension and retraction, and A (adventurous) motility based on focal adhesion (Chen and Nan, 2022), for which also slime extrusion at the trailing cell pole was earlier postulated as mechanism (Wolgemuth, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about myxobacteria, supported by multiple citations.

claim: S (social) motility in myxobacteria is based on pilus extension and retraction.
source: A few species appear to employ a type-IV-pilus-related mechanism (Khayatan et al., 2015; Wilde and Mullineaux, 2015), similar to the better-studied myxobacteria (Godwin et al., 1989; Mignot et al., 2007; Nan et al., 2014; Copenhagen et al., 2021; Godwin et al., 1989), which are short, rod-shaped single cells that exhibit two types of motility: S (social) motility based on pilus extension and retraction, and A (adventurous) motility based on focal adhesion (Chen and Nan, 2022), for which also slime extrusion at the trailing cell pole was earlier postulated as mechanism (Wolgemuth, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about myxobacterial motility, supported by citations.

claim: A (adventurous) motility in myxobacteria is based on focal adhesion.
source: A few species appear to employ a type-IV-pilus-related mechanism (Khayatan et al., 2015; Wilde and Mullineaux, 2015), similar to the better-studied myxobacteria (Godwin et al., 1989; Mignot et al., 2007; Nan et al., 2014; Copenhagen et al., 2021; Godwin et al., 1989), which are short, rod-shaped single cells that exhibit two types of motility: S (social) motility based on pilus extension and retraction, and A (adventurous) motility based on focal adhesion (Chen and Nan, 2022), for which also slime extrusion at the trailing cell pole was earlier postulated as mechanism (Wolgemuth, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about myxobacterial motility, supported by citations.

claim: Slime extrusion at the trailing cell pole was earlier postulated as a mechanism for myxobacterial A motility.
source: A few species appear to employ a type-IV-pilus-related mechanism (Khayatan et al., 2015; Wilde and Mullineaux, 2015), similar to the better-studied myxobacteria (Godwin et al., 1989; Mignot et al., 2007; Nan et al., 2014; Copenhagen et al., 2021; Godwin et al., 1989), which are short, rod-shaped single cells that exhibit two types of motility: S (social) motility based on pilus extension and retraction, and A (adventurous) motility based on focal adhesion (Chen and Nan, 2022), for which also slime extrusion at the trailing cell pole was earlier postulated as mechanism (Wolgemuth, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to scientific literature on myxobacterial motility mechanisms.

claim: Most gliding filamentous cyanobacteria do not exhibit visible pili.
source: Yet, most gliding filamentous cyanobacteria do not exhibit visible pili and their gliding mechanism appears to be distinct from myxobacteria (Khayatan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to scientific literature on cyanobacterial structures.

claim: The gliding mechanism of most filamentous cyanobacteria appears to be distinct from myxobacteria.
source: Yet, most gliding filamentous cyanobacteria do not exhibit visible pili and their gliding mechanism appears to be distinct from myxobacteria (Khayatan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to scientific literature comparing cyanobacterial and myxobacterial motility.

claim: Self-buckling is an important instability for self-propelling rod-like micro-organisms to change the orientation of their motion.
source: Self-Buckling is an important instability for self-propelling rod-like micro-organisms to change the orientation of their motion, enabling aggregation or the escape from traps (Fily et al., 2020; Man and Kanso, 2019; Isele-Holder et al., 2015; Isele-Holder et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific literature on self-buckling in microorganisms.

claim: Self-buckling enables aggregation or escape from traps in self-propelling rod-like micro-organisms.
source: Self-Buckling is an important instability for self-propelling rod-like micro-organisms to change the orientation of their motion, enabling aggregation or the escape from traps (Fily et al., 2020; Man and Kanso, 2019; Isele-Holder et al., 2015; Isele-Holder et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific literature on self-buckling behavior.

claim: The notion of self-buckling goes back to work of Leonhard Euler in 1780 on elastic columns subject to gravity.
source: The notion of self-buckling goes back to work of Leonhard Euler in 1780, who described elastic columns subject to gravity (Elishakoff, 2000).
evidence: This is historical knowledge about the origin of buckling theory, supported by a citation.

claim: Force and friction are strongly coupled in filamentous cyanobacteria, which favors an adhesion-based propulsion mechanism over the slime-extrusion hypothesis.
source: Force and friction are strongly coupled, which favors an adhesion-based propulsion mechanism (Khayatan et al., 2015; Wilde and Mullineaux, 2015) over the still customary slime-extrusion hypothesis (Hoiczyk and Baumeister, 1998; McBride, 2001).
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data showing coupling between force and friction, and is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The critical lengths found are close to the peak in the length distribution in freely growing colonies.
source: The critical lengths we found are close to the peak in the length distribution in freely growing colonies, indicating the importance of this quantity for their self-organization.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of measured critical lengths with observed length distributions.

claim: 388 collision events were collected for O. lutea.
source: In total, we collected 388 collision events for O. lutea and 280 for K. animale.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental data collected.

claim: 280 collision events were collected for K. animale.
source: In total, we collected 388 collision events for O. lutea and 280 for K. animale.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental data collected.

claim: Growth rather than velocity or force distributions most strongly impacts the buckling propensity of cyanobacterial colonies.
source: The natural length distribution (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), however, is very broad, and we conclude that growth rather than velocity or force distributions most strongly impacts the buckling propensity of cyanobacterial colonies.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the comparison of length distributions with velocity and force distributions.

claim: The buckling of gliding filaments differs from Euler's classical case in that propulsion forces are oriented tangentially instead of vertically.
source: The buckling of gliding filaments differs in two aspects: the propulsion forces are oriented tangentially instead of vertically, and the front end is supported instead of clamped.
evidence: This is a theoretical consideration distinguishing the current study from classical buckling theory.

claim: The buckling of gliding filaments differs from Euler's classical case in that the front end is supported instead of clamped.
source: The buckling of gliding filaments differs in two aspects: the propulsion forces are oriented tangentially instead of vertically, and the front end is supported instead of clamped.
evidence: This is a theoretical consideration distinguishing the current study from classical buckling theory.

claim: The friction is dominated by the lubrication drag from the contact with the substrate, filled by a thin layer of secreted polysaccharide slime.
source: Presumably, this friction is dominated by the lubrication drag from the contact with the substrate, filled by a thin layer of secreted polysaccharide slime which is much more viscous than the surrounding bulk fluid.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the source of friction, based on inference from the experimental setup.

claim: The polysaccharide slime layer is much more viscous than the surrounding bulk fluid.
source: Presumably, this friction is dominated by the lubrication drag from the contact with the substrate, filled by a thin layer of secreted polysaccharide slime which is much more viscous than the surrounding bulk fluid.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference about the properties of the slime layer.

claim: The motility mechanism might comprise adhering elements like pili or foci that increase the overall friction.
source: Speculatively, the motility mechanism might also comprise adhering elements like pili (Khayatan et al., 2015) or foci (Mignot et al., 2007) that increase the overall friction (Pompe et al., 2011).
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation, supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The drag due to the surrounding bulk fluid can be neglected.
source: Thus, the drag due to the surrounding bulk fluid can be neglected (Man and Kanso, 2019), and friction is assumed to be isotropic, a common assumption in motility models (Fei et al., 2020; Tchoufag et al., 2019; Wada et al., 2013).
evidence: This assumption is supported by citations to relevant literature on motility models.

claim: Friction is assumed to be isotropic.
source: Thus, the drag due to the surrounding bulk fluid can be neglected (Man and Kanso, 2019), and friction is assumed to be isotropic, a common assumption in motility models (Fei et al., 2020; Tchoufag et al., 2019; Wada et al., 2013).
evidence: This assumption is supported by citations to relevant literature on motility models.

claim: A homogeneous and constant distribution of an effectively tangential active force along the filament is assumed.
source: We assume a homogeneous and constant distribution of an effectively tangential active force along the filament.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption stated explicitly in the methods.

claim: Noise and fluctuations on the length scale of the individual cell are neglected.
source: Since many cells contribute simultaneously to the gliding force, one may expect noise and fluctuations on the length scale of the individual cell, far below the filament length, which we thus neglect.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption based on the scale of the system.

claim: A planar configuration and vanishing twist are assumed.
source: Based on our observations, we assume a planar configuration and a vanishing twist.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption based on experimental observations.

claim: Helical components of active force or friction are neglected.
source: Thus we also neglect any helical components of active force or friction, since these appear to merely add rigid-body rotation during free gliding.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption based on observations of the system behavior.

claim: The median active forces for the two species match almost perfectly.
source: Remarkably, the median active forces for the two species match almost perfectly.
evidence: This observation is based on the calculated force values from the experimental data.

claim: The similarity between the two species indicates a potential homology of their gliding apparati.
source: The similarity between the two species indicates a potential homology of their gliding apparati.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity in measured forces and friction coefficients.

claim: Friction is mainly isotropic in filamentous cyanobacteria.
source: This relation is remarkable in two aspects: On the one hand, it indicates that friction is mainly isotropic.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of friction coefficients measured in orthogonal directions.

claim: Friction is governed by an isotropic process like bond friction or lubrication from the slime layer in the contact with the substrate.
source: This suggests that friction is governed by an isotropic process like bond friction or lubrication from the slime layer in the contact with the substrate, the latter being consistent with the observation that mutations deficient in slime secretion do not glide but exogenous addition of slime restores motility (Khayatan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the isotropic nature of friction and supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Mutations deficient in slime secretion do not glide but exogenous addition of slime restores motility.
source: This suggests that friction is governed by an isotropic process like bond friction or lubrication from the slime layer in the contact with the substrate, the latter being consistent with the observation that mutations deficient in slime secretion do not glide but exogenous addition of slime restores motility (Khayatan et al., 2015).
evidence: This observation is cited from the literature and supports the role of slime in motility.

claim: Friction and propulsion forces correlate strongly despite being quite variable.
source: On the other hand, it indicates that friction and propulsion forces, despite being quite variable, correlate strongly.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing the relationship between force and friction.

claim: Generating more force comes at the expense of added friction.
source: Thus, generating more force comes, inevitably, at the expense of added friction.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed correlation between force and friction.

claim: For lubricated contacts, the friction coefficient is proportional to the thickness of the lubricating layer.
source: For lubricated contacts, the friction coefficient is proportional to the thickness of the lubricating layer (Snoeijer et al., 2013), and we conjecture active force and drag both increase due to a more intimate contact with the substrate.
evidence: This is established knowledge from fluid mechanics, supported by a citation.

claim: Active force and drag both increase due to a more intimate contact with the substrate.
source: For lubricated contacts, the friction coefficient is proportional to the thickness of the lubricating layer (Snoeijer et al., 2013), and we conjecture active force and drag both increase due to a more intimate contact with the substrate.
evidence: This is a conjecture based on the observed correlation and theoretical considerations.

claim: Mechanisms like focal adhesion or modified type-IV pilus generate forces through contact with extracellular surfaces.
source: This supports mechanisms like focal adhesion (Mignot et al., 2007) or a modified type-IV pilus (Khayatan et al., 2015), which generate forces through contact with extracellular surfaces, as the underlying mechanism of the gliding apparatus of filamentous cyanobacteria: more contacts generate more force, but also closer contact with the substrate, thereby increasing friction to the same extent.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: More contacts generate more force but also closer contact with the substrate, thereby increasing friction to the same extent.
source: This supports mechanisms like focal adhesion (Mignot et al., 2007) or a modified type-IV pilus (Khayatan et al., 2015), which generate forces through contact with extracellular surfaces, as the underlying mechanism of the gliding apparatus of filamentous cyanobacteria: more contacts generate more force, but also closer contact with the substrate, thereby increasing friction to the same extent.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation inferred from the observed correlation between force and friction.

claim: Force generation by slime extrusion would lead to the opposite behavior: more slime generates more propulsion but also reduces friction.
source: Force generation by slime extrusion (Hoiczyk and Baumeister, 1998), in contrast, would lead to the opposite behavior: More slime generates more propulsion, but also reduces friction.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about the expected behavior of slime extrusion mechanisms.

claim: Gliding velocity correlates positively with slime layer thickness.
source: Besides fundamental fluid-mechanical considerations (Snoeijer et al., 2013), this is rationalized by two experimental observations: i. gliding velocity correlates positively with slime layer thickness (Dhahri et al., 2013) and ii. motility in slime-secretion deficient mutants is restored upon exogenous addition of polysaccharide slime.
evidence: This observation is cited from the literature and supports the role of slime in motility.

claim: Small changes in the propulsion force density or the length distribution determine whether the majority of filaments in a colony is able to buckle or not.
source: As a consequence, small changes in the propulsion force density or the length distribution determine whether the majority of the filaments in a colony is able to buckle or not.
evidence: This is inferred from the relationship between critical length and the natural length distribution.

claim: The ample variety of non-equilibrium phases in active polymer melts may have contributed to the evolutionary success of filamentous cyanobacteria.
source: Thus, the ample variety of non-equilibrium phases in such materials (Isele-Holder et al., 2015; Isele-Holder et al., 2016; Prathyusha et al., 2018; Abbaspour et al., 2023) may well have contributed to the evolutionary success of filamentous cyanobacteria.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about evolutionary implications, supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Species Oscillatoria lutea (SAG 1459–3) and Kamptonema animale (SAG 1459–6) were obtained from The Culture Collection of Algae at Göttingen University.
source: Species Oscillatoria lutea (SAG 1459–3) and Kamptonema animale (SAG 1459–6) were obtained from The Culture Collection of Algae at Göttingen University and seeded in T175 culture flask with standard BG-11 nutrition solution.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the source of the organisms studied.

claim: The V-shape of the trap reduces the chance of filaments slipping sideways instead of buckling.
source: The V-shape is not necessarily required but reduces the chance of filaments slipping sideways instead of buckling, as was observed sometimes for collisions with flat walls.
evidence: This is an observation about the experimental design and its effects.

claim: The bending modulus values are comparable but slightly larger than values recently derived from cross-flow drag experiments.
source: Our values are comparable but slightly larger than values recently derived from cross-flow drag experiments (Faluweki and Goehring, 2022).
evidence: This is a comparison with values from the literature, supported by a citation.
